newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: OPPOSITION CRITICISES SUSPENSION OF INVITATION TO ARAFAT
The Federal Opposition says the decision to suspend an invitation to visit Australia to Palestinian President, Yasser Arafat, confirms the Government's erratic foreign policy performance.
Deputy Prime Minister, Tim Fischer, has confirmed he extended the invitation during a Middle East visit earlier this year.
Mr Fischer says he issued a number of invitations during his trip, and some have been withdrawn or suspended because the timing doesn't suit either the Australian or home Government.
Labor's Foreign Affairs spokesman, Laurie Brereton, says the Government's lurching from one foreign policy stuff-up to another.
Also demanding answers, the head of the Palestinian delegation to Australia, Ali Kazak.
He says he can't understand the Government's suspension of the invitation, because you don't invite a leader one day and change your mind the next.
The Government has confirmed Mr Fischer also invited Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to visit Australia, and this invitation hasn't been withdrawn.
BUSINESS LIQUIDATIONS FALL IN SOME STATES, RISE IN OTHERS
There's been a fall in business stress sales in Victoria, Tasmania and Queensland but the situation has worsened in New South Wales and the ACT.
The stress sales survey, compiled by the accounting firm Ernst and Young, counts the number of firms sold by receivers and liquidators.
Ernst and Young's Rick Dennis says that in the March quarter there was an increase of stress sales in the retail and wholesale sector, but things were brighter in manufacturing.
He says New South Wales and the ACT account for just over half of all stress sales reported in the quarter.
In that region, he says, the result has been fuelled mainly by an increase in the level of stress sale activity in the property and business services sector.
PRESSURE ON PROSSER CONTINUES TO MOUNT
The Federal Opposition claims Small Business Minister, Geoff Prosser, has effectively confirmed he has misled Parliament over his ministerial conduct, and now must resign.
Mr Prosser has been accused of breaching ministerial guidelines by calling Coles Myer Director, Nick Greiner, on behalf of his brother and business partner to seek a business contact name.
Labor claims Mr Prosser used the call to discuss the possibility of a Target store opening in one of his West Australian shopping centres.
In a statement to Parliament last night, Mr Prosser for the first time confirmed the call was in relation to the Target opportunity but said he never discussed the detail with Mr Greiner.
Labor's Small Business spokesman, Stephen Martin, has told A-B-C Radio this closes the case against Mr Prosser, because it means he has effectively admitted he misled parliament.
Mr Martin says there was only one thing missing from Mr Prosser's statement last night, and that was his resignation.
The Opposition's attack on Mr Prosser is expected to continue today.
DOLE VICTORY FOR GOVERNMENT
The Federal Government hopes to have its first work for the dole projects up and running by the end of the year, following the A-L-P's decision to reverse its opposition to the scheme.
Labor had combined with the Senate minor parties last week to impose a two-year time limit on the scheme.
However the government refused to accept the change and was threatening to use it to trigger a potential double dissolution election.
Opposition Leader, Kim Beazley, last night announced Labor will now allow the bill to pass through the Senate unamended when it returns to the Upper House later this week.
Training Minister David Kemp says he hopes the first projects will now be underway by October.
And he has described Labor's change of heart as a humiliating backdown, saying Labor has been out of touch with the community on this issue since the government's plans were announced.

On another front, the government last night used its numbers in the House of Representatives to formally reject the Senate's vote in favour of a voluntary postal ballot for Constitutional Convention delegates.
This brings the republic issue, to be debated by convention delegates, to a head, with Labor and the minor parties threatening to boycott the convention if the government does not concede.
VIC NURSES THREATEN TO RESUME INDUSTRIAL ACTION
Nurses have put the Victorian Government on notice of more industrial action, despite lifting bans on 1,200 public hospital beds.
The Australian Nursing Federation has entered a five week negotiating period with government and hospital officials.
While current workbans have been lifted, the A-N-F believes there could be insufficient government money to fund their 15 per cent pay claim.
State Secretary, Belinda Morieson, says if there is not a satisfactory outcome in five weeks, bans could be back on.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
